idiom_name: PAM: pam_start/pam_authenticate against a module stack configured in /etc/pam.d
implementation_notes: Linux-PAM is the canonical realization: the application opens a handle with pam_start() and calls pam_authenticate(), while the mechanism is chosen by the service's stack of modules (pam_unix, pam_ldap, pam_krb5, pam_u2f, ...) whose control flags (required, requisite, sufficient, optional) encode the chain semantics; the pam_conv conversation function carries prompts. The full hand-written structure (function-pointer table of mechanism callbacks plus a dispatcher) is only justified on platforms without PAM, or when the flow cannot be expressed as pam_authenticate/pam_acct_mgmt.
pitfalls: pam_authenticate() must not be retried in an application loop; the module stack's policy governs attempts (PAM_MAXTRIES).
Credential hygiene is the conversation function's job - the password buffer must be zeroed and never logged.
Stack order and control flags are security-relevant: a misplaced 'sufficient' entry turns a partial success into a full login.
PAM modules execute with the application's privileges, so a weak third-party module is a host-level risk.
